                         DIRECT TESTIMONY OF SHAWN MCGLOTHLIN

 1   Introduction, Qualifications and Summary

 2   Q     PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 3   A     Shawn McGlothlin; 14323 S. Outer 40 Rd., Suite 206N, Town & Country, Missouri

 4         63017.


 5   Q     WHAT IS YOUR OCCUPATION AND BY WHOM ARE YOU EMPLOYED?

 6   A     I am an Associate with J. Pollock, Incorporated.


 7   Q     PLEASE STATE YOUR EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND AND EXPERIENCE.

 8   A     I have a Bachelor of Science degree in Mechanical Engineering from Texas A&M

 9         University. Since joining J. Pollock, Incorporated in March 2024, I have worked on a

10         variety of regulatory proceedings in multiple states, including rate cases, system

11         resiliency plans, and cost recovery filings. Prior to that, I worked for nearly 29 years

12         at Texas Instruments Incorporated (TI), with my final years as TI’s Global Energy

13         Director.     As Global Energy Director, my scope included energy contracting and

14         hedging, strategic planning, sustainability execution and reporting, capital execution

15         support, and public policy support across TI’s global footprint. My qualifications are

16         documented in Appendix A. A list of my appearances is provided in Appendix B.


17   Q     ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU TESTIFYING IN THIS PROCEEDING?

18   A     I am testifying on behalf of Texas Industrial Energy Consumers (TIEC).


19   Q     WHAT ISSUES ARE YOU ADDRESSING IN YOUR DIRECT TESTIMONY?

20   A     I address issues pertaining to the Electric Service – Large Load (ES-LL) Contract

21         which Southwestern Electric Power Company (SWEPCO) proposes to incorporate into

22         its retail tariff.

 1   Q          IF YOUR TESTIMONY DOES NOT ADDRESS A PARTICULAR ISSUE, SHOULD

 2              THAT BE INTERPRETED AS AN ENDORSEMENT OF SWEPCO’S PROPOSAL?

 3   A          No.


 4   Q          PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR TESTIMONY.

 5   A          SWEPCO is proposing to add a new ES-LL Contract to its retail tariff to address the

 6              risk associated with potential unprecedented load growth, primarily as a result of new

 7              very large load (VLL) customers, such as data centers.1 As described by SWEPCO,

 8              the ES-LL Contract would place additional terms and conditions on these VLL

 9              customers to provide consistency, as well as protect SWEPCO and existing customers

10              against the risk these loads present.2

11                       In my testimony I will address several issues with SWEPCO’s proposed ES-LL

12              Contract which should be addressed as a condition of approval. Specifically, my

13              concerns are that SWEPCO’s proposal:

14                   1. Would place VLLs in the same customer class as existing Large Lighting
15                      and Power - Transmission (LLP-T) customers, notwithstanding that the
16                      very purpose of SWEPCO’s proposed ES-LL Contract is to address VLLs,
17                      which are unlike any customers SWEPCO currently serves; and
18                   2. Could be interpreted as forcing existing customers into ES-LL Contracts
19                      for engaging in normal business growth and is not tailored to address the
20                      unprecedented VLLs that are driving the proposal.

21              To address these concerns, I recommend that the Commission require SWEPCO to

22              treat ES-LL Contract customers as a separate customer class and, further, require

23              revisions to the ES-LL Contract applicability provisions.

 1   Q         PLEASE PROVIDE AN OVERVIEW OF SWEPCO’S PROPOSED ELECTRIC

 2             SERVICE – LARGE LOAD CONTRACT.

 3   A         SWEPCO’s ES-LL Contract is a three-page document which SWEPCO states is

 4             designed to address the multi-billion dollar investment risk associated with the large

 5             generation and networked transmission upgrades required to accommodate VLLs.3

 6             This is in contrast to SWEPCO’s Letter of Agreement (LOA), which is 13 pages and

 7             covers and secures direct interconnection costs and associated Contribution in Aid of

 8             Construction (CIAC) payments.4 While not explicitly stated by SWEPCO, it appears

 9             that the LOA and ES-LL Contract are designed to complement each other by

10             separately addressing generation and network transmission costs (ES-LL Contract)

11             and interconnection costs (LOA).

12                      The ES-LL Contract contains key provisions which would apply to any

13             customer whose aggregate load is greater than or equal to 75 megawatts (MW), such

14             as:

15                   • Ramp, Full Operations, and Billing Periods;
16                   • Initial Contract Term and Automatic Renewal Term;
17                   • Minimum Billing Demand and Energy Requirements; and,
18                   • Collateral Requirements and Termination Fees.5

19   Q         HAVE OTHER UTILITIES PROPOSED SPECIALIZED CONTRACTS TO ADDRESS

20             THE UNIQUE FEATURES OF LARGE LOADS?

21   A         Yes. SWEPCO states that its ES-LL Contract is similar to tariff provisions approved

22             for its AEP sister operating companies in Indiana, Kentucky, and West Virginia.6 In

 1          addition, as documented in the Database of Emerging Large Load Tariffs (DELTa)

 2          developed by the Smart Electric Power Alliance and North Carolina Clean Energy

 3          Technology Center, nearly every state commission has adopted, or is considering

 4          adopting, specific provisions to address the unique characteristics of large loads,

 5          including states such as Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Michigan, Minnesota, Kansas,

 6          Missouri, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Virginia, and Wisconsin.7


 7   Q      DOES SWEPCO'S PROPOSED ES-LL CONTRACT HAVE FEATURES SIMILAR

 8          TO THE VARIOUS LARGE LOAD TARIFFS APPROVED IN OTHER STATES?

 9   A      Yes, but only in a general sense. According to DELTa, most large load tariffs contain

10          provisions similar to SWEPCO’s ES-LL Contract including applicability, minimum term

11          length, ramp periods, minimum billing, termination fees, and financial assurance.

12          However, although the features of various large load tariffs are relatively consistent,

13          the specifics within each feature often vary widely.


14   Q      PLEASE ELABORATE ON THE WIDE VARIANCES AMONG LARGE LOAD

15          TARIFF PROVISIONS.

16   A      A few examples of the wide variances in the specific terms and conditions I noted in

17          my review of DELTa include:

18              • Contract term length variances of between 1 and 20 years, with some tariffs
19                allowing negotiable term lengths;
20              • Minimum load applicability variances of between 1 MW and 500 MW, with
21                some tariffs having an additional feature of a minimum load factor being
22                applied to recognize high load factors; and
23              • Financial assurance variances which range from collateral to CIAC; and
24                cover various combinations of generation, network transmission, and
25                interconnection costs.

 1   Q   WHAT DO YOU CONCLUDE FROM YOUR REVIEW OF LARGE LOAD TARIFF

 2       PROVISIONS IN DELTA?

 3   A   Large load tariffs have similar features at the surface, but that similarity breaks down

 4       once specifics are compared. In my opinion, there are unique circumstances driving

 5       the variances in each proceeding, such as state policies or specific characteristics of

 6       the utility. Further, large loads are an emerging issue with little historical reference —

 7       thus, it appears to me that many of the tariffs are also being driven by the need to

 8       accommodate one or more specific new large loads seeking to interconnect. As a

 9       result, each tariff reflects a combination of policy, utility concerns, and the unique

10       characteristics of high probability VLL customers seeking to interconnect.


11   Q   SHOULD SWEPCO’S ES-LL CONTRACT BE ADOPTED BASED ON ITS

12       SIMILARITY TO OTHER AEP SISTER OPERATING COMPANY TARIFFS?

13   A   No. A broader review of the tariff provisions adopted across the various jurisdictions

14       reveals a much wider variance in approach than does focusing on the provisions

15       adopted by AEP’s sister operating companies alone. In my opinion, this reflects that

16       we are in the early stages of the data center industry’s growth, and tariffs will need to

17       continue evolving as regulators grapple with how best to treat these unprecedented

18       loads.   Given the state of flux in this industry, and the potential for subsequent

19       regulatory and legislative developments, the Commission may need to revisit how best

20       to address VLLs in SWEPCO’s territory in the future. However, the focus of this

21       proceeding should be to protect SWEPCO’s existing customers while enabling specific

22       high confidence VLL projects to move forward.

 1   Q         WHAT IS YOUR RECOMMENDATION?

 2   A         The Commission should not simply accept an ES-LL Contract that adopts features

 3             similar to other tariffs. Instead, the Commission should apply specific requirements

 4             based on the VLL projects driving SWEPCO’s ES-LL Contract proposal.


 5   Rate Schedule Treatment of ES-LL Customers

 6   Q         HOW DOES SWEPCO PROPOSE TO CLASSIFY CUSTOMERS SUBJECT TO AN

 7             ES-LL CONTRACT?

 8   A         SWEPCO is not proposing to create a new customer class for ES-LL customers at this

 9             time.8 Instead, SWEPCO proposes to include ES-LL customers under the existing

10             LLP-T rate schedule.9

11   Q         WHAT IS YOUR CONCERN WITH SWEPCO’S PROPOSAL TO CLASSIFY ES-LL

12             CONTRACT CUSTOMERS AS LLP-T CUSTOMERS?

13   A         In a class cost-of-service study, costs are allocated to customer classes, which are

14             typically comprised of customers having similar characteristics, such as size, delivery

15             voltage, load factor, coincidence factor, and firmness. SWEPCO has not demonstrated

16             potential ES-LL Contract customers have similar characteristics as LLP-T

17             customers.10 Instead, SWEPCO simply asserts that the LLP-T rate schedule is

18             designed for large, high load factor loads.11

 1   Q        IS THERE EVIDENCE THAT POTENTIAL ES-LL CONTRACT CUSTOMERS ARE

 2            LIKELY TO TAKE SERVICE DIFFERENTLY THAN EXISTING LLP-T CUSTOMERS,

 3            CONTRARY TO SWEPCO’S ASSERTION?

 4   A        Yes. First and most obvious is the order of magnitude difference in load size. The

 5            average existing LLP-T customer has a non-coincident peak demand of 32 MW, and

 6            no existing customers are above 75 MW.12 By contrast, SWEPCO has a signed LOA

 7            with at least one 500 MW ES-LL Contract customer and performed contract studies

 8            for loads up to 1,500 MW.13 Adding even one 500 MW ES-LL Contract customer to

 9            the existing LLP-T customer class would more than quadruple the size of that

10            customer class.14 As a result, even relatively minor differences in how service is taken

11            between existing LLP-T customers and ES-LL Contract customers would be

12            magnified.

13                   Second, SWEPCO’s proposal assumes that ES-LL Contract customers are

14            high load factor, with load factors of approximately 85%.15 By contrast, existing LLP-

15            T customers operate at an average 54% load factor.16

 1                     Third, some existing LLP-T customers take all, or a portion, of their service

 2             under Standby, Maintenance, and As-Available rates. As service is required only to

 3             replace the capacity and energy normally provided by on-site generation, which occurs

 4             infrequently, it is unlikely that the peak demands of these customers would occur

 5             coincident with SWEPCO’s system peak. By contrast, VLLs are associated with data

 6             centers that operate around the clock. Thus, their peak demands are more likely to

 7             occur coincident with SWEPCO’s system peak.


 8   Q         WHAT DO YOU RECOMMEND TO RESOLVE YOUR CONCERN?

 9   A         Because SWEPCO currently has no ES-LL Contract customers, has provided no

10             analysis of potential customers under that contract, and there is ample evidence of

11             significant differences between existing LLP-T customers and potential ES-LL

12             Contract customers, the Commission should require SWEPCO to treat ES-LL Contract

13             customers as a separate customer class. This will ensure that any decision regarding

14             the classification of ES-LL Contract customers is thoroughly reviewed in a future

15             proceeding designed to weigh such matters, such as a rate case.


16   ES-LL Contract

17   Q         WHAT IS SWEPCO’S PURPOSE IN PROPOSING THE ES-LL CONTRACT?

18   A         SWEPCO states that it is facing an “unprecedented” amount of large load demand

19             consisting of “pending and anticipated requests from large load customers for new

20             electric service.”17 However, its existing Contract for Electric Service “does not provide

21             the protections needed for non-large load customers and the Company against the

 1              inherent risks associated with adding incremental large loads.”18            Accordingly,

 2              SWEPCO asserts that it is necessary to adopt an ES-LL contract “to provide consistent

 3              and reasonable terms of service to these anticipated large load customers, while

 4              ensuring existing customers and the Company are protected against the inherent risks

 5              associated with these loads.”19


 6   Q          WHAT CONCLUSIONS DO YOU DRAW FROM SWEPCO’S STATED PURPOSE?

 7   A          First, if the purpose of the contract is to protect existing customers, then the contract

 8              should be clear that it does not apply to existing customers. Second, SWEPCO’s

 9              concerns are with new loads of unprecedented magnitude that its existing tariffs and

10              contracts are not designed to address; therefore, the contract should focus on those

11              new types of loads. Accordingly, the new ES-LL Contract should be targeted at the

12              new and unprecedented large loads approaching SWEPCO, and not inadvertently

13              include traditional large loads which SWEPCO, and other utilities across Texas, have

14              been successfully serving for many years.


15   Q          WHAT IS YOUR CONCERN REGARDING THE APPLICABILITY SECTION OF THE

16              PROPOSED ES-LL CONTRACT AS IT PERTAINS TO EXISTING CUSTOMERS?

17   A          As written, the Applicability section could be interpreted as inadvertently forcing

18              existing customers into an ES-LL Contract. The relevant language is as follows:

19                    This form of contract (CONTRACT FOR ELECTRIC SERVICE TEXAS –
20                    LARGE LOAD) shall apply to any customer whose Contract Capacity (per
21                    Schedule 1 below), whether for any single facility or for multiple facilities in
22                    aggregate, is greater than or equal to 75 MW.20

 1            As can be seen, there is no specific statement in the contract excluding existing

 2            customers or limiting the 75 MW threshold to new incremental load. As written, any

 3            customer, including an existing customer, who load exceeds 75 MW could be forced

 4            into an ES-LL Contract. Further, VLLs are known to be large concentrated loads, yet

 5            SWEPCO proposes to aggregate loads which may individually be much smaller.


 6   Q        DOES SWEPCO INTEND TO APPLY THE ES-LL CONTRACT TO ALL CUSTOMER

 7            LOADS GREATER THAN 75 MW?

 8   A        No. SWEPCO stated in discovery that the ES-LL Contract would not apply to any

 9            existing customers.21 Further, SWEPCO confirms that its intent would be to apply the

10            75 MW threshold to new incremental load growth, without including existing customer

11            load.22 Thus, this appears to be an issue which can be corrected by stating this

12            explicitly in the contract.


13   Q        DO YOU HAVE ANY ADDITIONAL CONCERNS WITH THE APPLICABILITY

14            LANGUAGE CONTAINED IN SWEPCO’S PROPOSED ES-LL CONTRACT?

15   A        Yes. As noted earlier, SWEPCO’s stated purpose in proposing this contract is to

16            address unprecedented new large loads that SWEPCO believes present new and

17            unaddressed risks. However, SWEPCO’s 75 MW threshold for applicability appears

18            to be inconsistent with this purpose, particularly under the circumstances of this case.

19            In my opinion, and as explained earlier, a 75 MW threshold could capture loads, such

20            as traditional industrial loads, that are not creating the risks which SWEPCO proposes

21            to address.

 1   Q   ARE THERE ANY DIFFERENCES BETWEEN THE RISKS POSED BY

 2       TRADITIONAL INDUSTRIAL LOADS AND THE LARGE LOADS WHICH SWEPCO

 3       IS ADDRESSING?

 4   A   There can be. As I understand it, the new large loads driving SWEPCO’s need are

 5       large and concentrated data center loads. As compared to traditional industrial loads,

 6       data center loads at this scale are a recent phenomenon; and, further, this industry is

 7       developing at a very rapid pace. As a result, regulators and utilities do not have the

 8       same history in dealing with these concentrated computational loads as they have with

 9       traditional industrial loads. Further, data centers tend to be less tied to a specific

10       geographic region, whereas industrial loads are often tied to a specific location or

11       region in order to access resources that cannot be readily found elsewhere. For

12       instance, an oil and gas developer is tied to the location where those minerals are

13       located, and manufacturing and petrochemical loads often require proximity to ports

14       or other transportation hubs. Further, developing a large industrial site (such as a

15       refinery or factory) tends to be extremely complex and the resulting facility tends to be

16       very difficult (if not essentially impossible) to relocate.


17   Q   ARE     THERE      EXAMPLES         OF     REGULATORY         DEVELOPMENTS         THAT

18       RECOGNIZE THESE DIFFERENCES?

19   A   Yes. First, as discussed further below, some large load tariffs set a substantially larger

20       threshold than the 75 MW threshold SWEPCO proposes.               Further, some recent

21       proposals go further and tie the applicability of certain requirements to the end use of

22       the customer, not just the load size. For example, ERCOT recently adopted frequency

23       and voltage ride-through requirements that only apply to “Large Computational

 2             between “computational” loads and “non-computational” loads.24


 3   Q         IS SWEPCO’S PROPOSED 75 MW THRESHOLD CONSISTENT WITH THE AEP

 4             TARIFFS UPON WHICH IT RELIES?

 5   A         No. SWEPCO compares its proposal to the large load tariffs adopted by four of its

 6             sister companies within AEP, all of which establish a minimum demand threshold at

 7             150 MW.25 Thus, based on SWEPCO’s own logic, it would be more reasonable to set

 8             the minimum demand threshold at 150 MW, instead of 75 MW. However, as I noted

 9             earlier, there are wide variances across the approved tariffs in other states which, in

10             my opinion, indicate that each state commission is considering the unique

11             circumstances driving the need for a large load tariff.


12   Q         WHAT ARE SWEPCO’S UNIQUE CIRCUMSTANCES WHICH SHOULD BE

13             CONSIDERED         BEFORE       DETERMINING        APPLICABILITY        OF       AN   ES-LL

14             CONTRACT?

15   A         An important consideration should be to only include the loads that are causing the

16             need for the new contract. In this instance, SWEPCO only has one signed LOA in

17             Texas – a 500 MW load. Further, of the nine contract studies SWEPCO has done in

18             Texas, seven are for 500 to 1,500 MW loads.26 Thus, SWEPCO’s current need for an

19             ES-LL Contract is not driven by disaggregated loads that total 75 MW or greater, but

 4   Q         WHAT     DO    YOU     PROPOSE       TO    ADDRESS       YOUR     ES-LL    CONTRACT

 5             APPLICABILITY LANGUAGE CONCERNS?

 6   A         The ES-LL Contract should be modified to have an applicability threshold higher than

 7             SWEPCO proposes and limited to a single facility. Specifically, for purposes of this

 8             case, I propose that the ES-LL Contract apply to only new incremental loads of no less

 9             than 250 MW at a single facility. Defining applicability this way will easily capture the

10             large concentrated loads at issue without inadvertently including existing customers

11             whose loads are not driving the need for the ES-LL Contract.


12   Q         DO RECENT DEVELOPMENTS IN ERCOT SUPPORT ADOPTING SWEPCO’S

13             PROPOSED 75 MW THRESHOLD?

14   A         No. As an initial matter, SWEPCO is not in ERCOT and regulations adopted for

15             ERCOT do not apply to SWEPCO who is the Southwest Power Pool. Further, while

16             Senate Bill 6 created a 75 MW threshold in ERCOT to establish the guidelines for

17             certain financial and study requirements, that legislation did not mandate rate

18             structures or include specific contractual terms.28 Further, the Commission is actively

19             considering whether thresholds higher than 75 MW can be appropriate depending on

20             the circumstances. For example, in the pending Project No. 58481, the proposal for

21             publication would establish different levels of study fees for loads of 250 MW and

 4   Q      DO YOU HAVE PROPOSED LANGUAGE FOR THE APPLICABILITY SECTION OF

 5          THE ES-LL CONTRACT THAT WOULD ADDRESS YOUR CONCERNS?

 6   A      Yes, the Applicability section should be modified as follows:

 7              This form of contract (CONTRACT FOR ELECTRIC SERVICE TEXAS –
 8              LARGE LOAD) shall apply to any customer whose new incremental load after
 9              the revision date of this contract, as reflected in Contract Capacity (per
10              Schedule 1 below), whether for any at a single facility or for multiple facilities
11              in aggregate, is greater than or equal to 75 250 MW.

12   Q      DO YOU HAVE ANY ADDITIONAL COMMENTS ON THE PROVISIONS OF

13          SWEPCO’S PROPOSED ES-LL?

14   A      Yes, I note that many of the definitions and features of the contract are not fully defined.

15          For example, the proposed ES-LL Contract proposes a Ramp Period during which the

16          customer load is increasing towards its Full Operations Period and would not be

17          charged based on its full contract demand. However, the proposed ES-LL Contract

18          does not specify the maximum length of the Ramp Period or discuss whether or not

19          there would be flexibility to modify the Ramp Period within that period. Similarly, the

20          proposed ES-LL Contract proposes enhanced Collateral Requirements but does not

21          specify things such as the form of collateral, credit rating, financial liquidity

22          requirements, or measures SWEPCO will take to verify that the requirements are met
